paras: The Red Bank lynching threat of July 1903 was a threatened lynching in Red Bank, New Jersey, on July 14, 1903, when a crowd gathered at the town lockup after Thomas Thomas, alias Thomas Drum, a Black ex-convict, was arrested on charges of burglarizing the home of Mayor O. E. Davis and attempting to assault his daughter, Grace Davis. Police hurried the prisoner to the county jail at Freehold, and no attempt was made to seize him. He was indicted two days later and convicted within a week, and several white papers held up the case as an example of law prevailing over mob violence.

Thomas had worked for Davis, a former sheriff of Monmouth County, painting houses and doing odd jobs, according to the New York Sun. The Sun and the Monmouth Inquirer both described a past prison term for incendiary fires in Red Bank, and the Sun said he had been paroled about two years earlier from a thirty-year sentence.

In the early hours of Tuesday, July 14, an intruder entered the Davis house on Riverside Avenue through a porch window, took jewelry and a pocketbook, and attacked Grace Davis, who was eighteen, in her bedroom. The Sun said the man threatened to kill her and struck her repeatedly when she screamed, while the Inquirer described a single blow to the forehead. Her father raised the alarm, and Police Captain William H. Wilson, called Chief Wilson in the county paper, and neighbors followed stocking footprints through the mud to a barn owned by Davis, where Thomas was found in the hayloft with another Black man, Daniel Webster. The Inquirer reported that jewelry belonging to Grace Davis was found in Thomas's clothing.

According to the Sun, a crowd of about fifty gathered around the lockup some four hours after the attack, and one businessman told Wilson that there would be a lynching if the prisoner was not taken out of town before night. The New-York Tribune reported that some of the most excited residents declared Thomas should be burned at the stake. The Sun added that no move was made to capture him, but Wilson sent both men by train to the Freehold jail.

The Monmouth County grand jury indicted Thomas on July 16; he pleaded not guilty, and counsel was assigned because he had no money for a lawyer. Webster was not indicted but remained in custody. On July 20 a jury at Freehold convicted Thomas on two indictments, for breaking and entering and for assault with intent to commit burglary, after five minutes of deliberation. He was sentenced to nineteen years and also had to serve sixteen unexpired years of his earlier term, thirty-five years in all.

The Associated Press dispatch ran under headlines such as "Lynch Talk in New Jersey" and credited the police with averting trouble by hurrying Thomas out of town. The New York papers gave the story more space: the Sun headed it "Lynching Feared in Jersey" and called Thomas a "bad nigger" when drinking, while the Tribune compared the excitement to that over the "Mingo Jack" lynching at Eatontown some fifteen years earlier. The Monmouth Inquirer, the county paper, treated the case as a burglary and did not mention a crowd or lynching talk.

After the conviction, editorial writers used Red Bank as a lesson. The Providence News wrote that such prompt punishment was "a far greater deterrent than any lynching," and the Newark News paired Red Bank with a Hackensack case as proof of "Jersey justice" and of the preference for law over mob violence. The Mobile Register took a different line, citing a Sun page on assaults near Red Bank, Trenton and Albany to suggest that Northerners would discover the "difficulties" of the issue now that it came close to home.

bases: A threatened lynching: a crowd of about fifty gathered at the lockup and a businessman warned of a lynching, and residents talked of burning the prisoner, who was removed to the county jail (A1, A2, A3).

The Sun, the Tribune's special and the AP wire independently report lynching talk and the prisoner's hurried removal to Freehold (A1, A2, A3); the county paper confirms the arrest and removal but not the crowd (A4).

Sun headline 'Lynching Feared in Jersey' with a detailed crime story using 'bad nigger'; reports the threat without comment.
Providence News and Newark News editorials favor prompt courts over lynching and praise 'Jersey justice'.
Mobile Register editorial uses the Red Bank case to say Northerners will discover the 'difficulties' of the issue.
